questions.q: What is the ITIL 4 purpose of the change enablement practice?
options: To maximize the number of successful service and product changes by ensuring risks are properly assessed
To minimize the total number of changes made to production systems
To restore normal service operation as quickly as possible
To identify the root cause of recurring incidents
questions.explain: The purpose is more successful changes through proper risk assessment, not fewer changes overall.

questions.q: Why did ITIL 4 rename "change management" to "change enablement"?
options: To avoid confusion with organizational change management, the separate discipline of helping people adapt to new ways of working
Because change management no longer involves any risk assessment
Because ITIL 4 removed authorization requirements from the practice
Because standard changes were eliminated in ITIL 4
questions.explain: The rename specifically distinguishes IT change enablement from organizational change management, which deals with people, not systems.

questions.q: What makes a change a "standard change"?
options: It is low-risk, well-understood, and has been performed successfully many times before, so it's pre-authorized
It must be implemented as soon as possible to resolve a major incident
It requires review by the most senior change authority available
It has never been performed before and carries unknown risk
questions.explain: Standard changes follow a known, proven procedure, which is why they don't need individual sign-off every time.

questions.q: What distinguishes a normal change from a standard change?
options: A normal change needs individual assessment and authorization through a defined process, rather than being pre-authorized
A normal change never requires any authorization at all
A normal change is always implemented faster than a standard change
A normal change is only used to fix major incidents
questions.explain: Normal changes haven't been proven safe by repetition, so each one is individually assessed and authorized, often scheduled around risk and impact.

questions.q: An engineer needs to implement an emergency change to resolve a major incident. According to ITIL 4, what should still happen before it's implemented?
options: An expedited but still-real authorization step, even if full documentation is completed afterward
Nothing — emergency changes skip authorization entirely by definition
The change must wait for the next scheduled change advisory board meeting
The change must first be reclassified as a standard change
questions.explain: Emergency changes are fast, but ITIL 4 is explicit that they still require authorization — just an expedited version of the normal process.
